comments.text_zh: 我有个问题想问 HN：从什么时候起，你要为自己的教育负责？以前，你身边可能没有公共图书馆。如今，信息太多了。内容筛选？多个 MOOC 已经接手这个问题并把它解决了。网络接入？我不确定，但我记得读到过 Comcast 在低收入地区提供补贴费率。电脑／笔记本？这个我完全不确定。人们能获得什么资源？假设人们能接触到教育，那么从什么时候起“教育者”就不再必要了？我觉得如果这些 MOOC 当时就有，我可能就不会去上高中了。不过，我确实有足够的个人好奇心去追求这些东西。现在上了大学，我不再被“喂到嘴边”了，学好是我的责任，如果遇到困难，我得主动去寻求帮助。我只是好奇大家认为这条线该划在哪里，以及它对每个人是否不同。我要去考 Bar exam——天哪，居然还有老师在试图教授神创论！这是我最喜欢的关于教育改革的一个视频，来自 Sir Ken Robinson，视角非常合乎逻辑。附赠：它还是图画动画的！[视频]
comments.text: I have a question for HN. At what point do you become responsible for your own education? Before, you may have not had a public library near you. Nowadays, there is too much information. Curation? Multiple MOOC's have taken the problem and squashed it. Internet Access? I'm not sure, but I remember reading that Comcast gives subsidized rates in poor income areas. Computers / Notebooks? This I'm not sure about at all. What access do people have? Assuming people have access to education, at what point are "educators" defunct? I feel as though I would not have gone to high school had these MOOC's been available. However, I did have enough personal curiosity to pursue these things. In college now, I'm not "spoon fed" anymore, it is my responsibility to do well, and seek out help if I am struggling. I am just curious where people think that line is drawn, and if it's different for everyone or not. I am for the Bar exam - for goodness's sake, we still have teachers trying to teach Creationism! One of my favorite videos on reforming education, from a very logical perspective from Sir Ken Robinson. Bonus: it's pictorially animated! [VIDEO]

Instead of forcing children to think one way, we should let them think the way they NATURALLY think, and flourish with their native mindset. comments.text_zh: 我完全同意，而且我对公共教育系统如此失望，以至于现在正纠结该为我的孩子选择什么才是正确答案。我理解很多孩子不是这样，但我就是那种在小学时读物理教科书的孩子。我们有一个导师计划，会把孩子和高两个年级的人配对（比如一年级配三年级）。我的阅读水平一直比我的导师高，这让我很愤怒（可能也很讨人厌）。我觉得我在学校的全部时间都花在把它应付过去上，好让我能去学真正让我感兴趣的东西。我很希望我的孩子不要感受到同样的限制，而是能自由地按自己的节奏深入下去。我推荐 Sir Ken Robinson 关于这个话题的这场演讲：[VIDEO]
comments.text: I wholeheartedly agree, and came out so disillusioned with the public education system that I'm struggling to decide what the right answer will be for my children. I understand that many kids are not this way, but I was the type that read physics textbooks while in elementary school. We had a mentorship program that paired kids with someone from two grades above (e.g. 1st graders with 3rd graders). My reading level was always higher than my mentors' and it made me furious (and probably insufferable). I feel like my entire time in school was spent getting it out of the way so I could study things that genuinely interested me. I would love for my children to not feel that same constraint, but instead feel free to go deeper at their own pace. I'd recommend this talk by Sir Ken Robinson on this topic generally: [VIDEO]

comments.text_zh: 关于这个话题有很多学术文章和研究，比如 [链接]。显然，其中一部分差异会被以前不存在的新职业吸收掉。例如，这里有一份 10 年前还不存在的职业清单 [链接]。我确信繁荣是由贸易和专业化推动的，正如 Matt Ridley 所提出的 [链接]。专业化是一种技能，所以问题实质上是非熟练劳动力会怎样。每个人“都知道”教育是解决办法，但当前的教育体系极其破败，而且基本上是照着工业时代初期塑造出来的 [视频]。生活成本是否会下降，这值得关注，因为那也会大大缓解问题。自动化程度提高应该会带来这一结果。
comments.text: There are many academic pieces and work on the topic such as [LINK] Obviously some of the difference will be soaked up by new professions that didn't exist before. For example here is a list of jobs that didn't exist 10 years ago [LINK] I am convinced that prosperity is being driven by trade and specialisation as put forward by Matt Ridley [LINK] Specialisation is a form of skill and so the issue is really what happens to unskilled labour. Everyone "knows" that education is a fix, but current education systems are extremely broken and closely modelled on the dawn of the industrial age [VIDEO] It will be interesting to see if the cost of living goes down since that will also greatly alleviate things. Increased automation should result in that.

comments.text_zh: 这个故事的整个前提让我不得不戴上锡箔帽。[tldr] [LINK] 问题太多，答案太少。我先从最直接的想法说起。高辍学率绝对不一定是坏事。事实上，在所有完全不关注“如何学习”的西方学校里，这相当正常。这个“问题”显然出在教育体系更早的阶段：学生到了上大学年龄却不知道“如何学习”，然后突然发现这很重要。接下来是学习/知识材料的成本。我知道美国有些教科书定价高达数千美元（或者干脆不供学生购买）。“老师/讲师”没那么重要（我这么说，是因为我从英国一所顶尖大学以联合一等荣誉学位毕业，期间收到过很多警告，批评我几乎从不去上课；但我跳过的不是材料，而是那些照着教科书念的讲师）。话虽如此，我总觉得这些故事更像是在攻击那种为美国下层阶级提供成为中产和上层阶级机会的教育。这个 ITT Tech 的故事没有任何内容从任一方向回应这一点。那些成功毕业的人的就业数据在哪里？对毕业生的采访在哪里？我只看到大量夸张的“他说她说”。每当我遇到这种情况，我都会自动认为这是基于政治权力的决定，而不是理性的“对所有人都有好处”的决定。我知道这一切听起来有点混乱——
comments.text: This whole premise of this story has me wearing a tin foil hat. [tldr] [LINK] Soooo many questions. so few answers. I'll start with my immediate thoughts. High dropouts are not absolutely a bad thing. In fact its pretty normal in all western schools that have zero focus on "how to learn". The "problem" is clearly earlier on in the education system, wherby students are reaching college age not knowing "how to learn", and suddenly finding its important. Next up - the cost of learning/knowledge material. I know of textbooks from the US being priced in the multi thousand dollar range (or simply not available for student purchase). "Teachers/Lecturers" aren't that important (I say that having graduated with a joint 1st from a top UK university having acquired a lot of warnings criticizing me for hardly ever attending lectures, but I wasn't skipping the material, I was skipping lecturers reading from textbooks). All that said, I am left feeling these stories are more about attacking education that provides chances for the lower classes in the US to become middle and upper classes. Nothing about this ITT tech story addresses this one way or the other. Where are the employment stats for those who successfully graduate? Where are the interviews with graduates? I just see a ton of hyperbole he said she said. And whenever I come across that I automatically assume its a political power based decision, rather than a rational "good for everyone" one. I know that all sounds a bit confused -
